knowledge: Tokens are model-specific units: newer models can use a different tokenizer that produces more tokens for the same text, so counts never transfer across model generations.
Everything in a request counts toward the context window: system prompt, all messages (including tool results), tool definitions, and the output generated for the turn, including thinking.
The model generates one token at a time, each conditioned only on earlier tokens, so a verdict written before the reasoning cannot depend on that reasoning.
Output is sampled, so identical inputs can give different outputs; current models reject `temperature`, `top_p` and `top_k`, so consistency comes from prompt and output design, not sampling knobs.

Adaptive thinking lets the model decide per request whether and how much to think, steered mainly by `effort`; effort affects all output tokens (text, tool calls, thinking), and thinking is billed as output even when only a summary is shown.
Fast mode (`speed: "fast"` on supported models) raises output tokens per second at premium pricing; it does not target time to first token and is not available with the Batch API.
skills: Pick zero-shot for clear, common tasks and add 3 to 5 diverse examples (multi-shot) when format, tone or edge cases must be matched.
Diagnose single-shot over-imitation (copied length or details) and fix it with varied examples.

examLens: Inconsistent output: constrain the output and add examples, then measure with repeated-run evals; never rely on a seed or zero temperature.

knowledge: Official SDKs wrap the REST API with typed request and response models, typed error classes mapped from HTTP status codes, and auth read from configuration (default `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`).
SDKs automatically retry connection errors, 408, 409, 429 and 5xx responses a small number of times with exponential backoff; `max_retries` and `timeout` are configurable per client or per request.
SDKs reject non-streaming requests expected to run longer than roughly ten minutes; streaming (or an explicit timeout override) is the documented fix.

The Messages API streams over HTTP using server-sent events (`stream: true`): `message_start`, content block start/delta/stop, `message_delta` with cumulative usage, then `message_stop`; errors such as overload can arrive mid-stream.
WebSockets are bidirectional and full-duplex; they belong between your browser and your backend when users must send signals mid-stream, not between your backend and the Claude API.
Every response carries a request ID (exposed by the SDK, for example `_request_id` in Python) for debugging and support.
skills: Configure SDK auth, timeouts and retries centrally instead of stacking custom retry loops.
Classify errors with SDK error classes: retry transient ones, fail fast on bad-request and auth errors.

Read response content by block `type` rather than assuming the first block is text.
examLens: Prefer the SDK's built-in retries, typed errors and stream helpers over hand-rolled equivalents.
The API key never reaches the browser or a mobile client; the backend calls Claude.
Long generations: stream them; do not lower `max_tokens` below what the task needs.
Usage from a stream: take the cumulative value, do not sum `message_delta` events.
traps: Claiming the Claude API streams over WebSockets or requires polling.
Wrapping SDK calls in another retry loop that also retries permanent 400 and 401 errors.
Indexing `content[0].text` and breaking once thinking or tool-use blocks appear.

knowledge: Haiku is the fastest, lowest-cost tier for high-volume, latency-sensitive work such as classification, extraction, routing and subagent tasks.
Sonnet is positioned as the best combination of speed and intelligence for everyday coding, agent and enterprise workloads.
Opus targets complex, long-running agentic coding and knowledge work where accuracy outweighs cost and latency.
Effort trades intelligence for latency and cost within one model, and tuning it is often a better lever than switching models.
A model ID is a pinned snapshot; new releases ship under new IDs and can bring breaking changes (rejected parameters, prefill errors, new tokenizers) documented in migration guides.
Adaptive thinking is supported only on newer models; older models that support only extended thinking reject `type: "adaptive"` with a 400 error.
skills: Match a workload's quality, latency and cost constraints to a starting tier, efficiency-first or capability-first.
Use an eval set to compare tiers and effort levels, then adopt the cheapest configuration that clears the bar.
Plan an upgrade: keep the pinned ID, run evals, and work through the migration guide before switching traffic.
Recount tokens and update cost models when moving to a model with a different tokenizer.
Make thinking configuration model-aware in shared client code.
examLens: The right model is the cheapest one that meets the quality bar on your own evals, not the biggest one.
Before downgrading tiers to save money, try lowering effort on the current model.
Upgrades are tested changes: pin, evaluate, migrate; never auto-follow the newest model in production.
traps: Treating public benchmark gains as enough evidence to switch production.
Assuming new models are backward compatible with old parameters and token counts.
Picking the largest model, or the smallest, without considering the stated constraint.

knowledge: `usage` splits input into `input_tokens` (after the last cache breakpoint), `cache_read_input_tokens` and `cache_creation_input_tokens`; total input is their sum.
Cache reads are billed at a fraction of base input price, cache writes at a premium over base input, and output (including thinking) at the higher output rate.

The cache prefix is built in the order `tools`, `system`, `messages`; a change at one level invalidates that level and everything after it, and changing speed, thinking or effort settings can also invalidate parts of the cache.
Cache hits require an identical prefix up to the breakpoint within the cache lifetime; writes happen only at breakpoints, and lookup checks a limited window of earlier blocks.
Prompts below a model's minimum cacheable length are silently not cached; both cache fields reading 0 is the signal.
Token counting is free (rate-limited), returns an estimate, and does not apply caching.
skills: Build cost dashboards and forecasts from every `usage` field priced at its own rate.
Place `cache_control` on the last block whose prefix stays identical, with dynamic content after it.
Add intermediate breakpoints (check-points) in long agent turns so earlier cache entries stay reachable.
Diagnose cache misses caused by timestamps, per-request tool changes or settings toggles.
Choose between automatic caching and explicit breakpoints, and between the default and longer TTL, based on traffic patterns.
examLens: Stable content first, volatile content last, breakpoint on the last stable block.

If cache writes happen every request, something in the prefix changes; find it before adding more breakpoints.
traps: Reading only `input_tokens` after enabling caching and concluding context shrank.
Putting per-user tools or timestamps early in the prefix.
Assuming cache reads cost the same as or more than base input.
